description: Learn to extract the exact data you need from messy HTML using BeautifulSoup and XPath.

slides.title: Introduction to Parsing
slides.content:
# The Messy Web 🕸️

When you use `requests` to get a webpage, you get back one giant string of HTML.

Extracting data from that string using regular expressions or string splitting is a nightmare, because HTML is often broken, deeply nested, or randomly formatted.

To solve this, we use **Parsers**.
A Parser takes raw HTML and converts it into a navigable tree structure (the Document Object Model, or DOM).

slides.title: BeautifulSoup4
slides.content:
# Beautiful Soup 🍲 `BeautifulSoup4` (BS4) is the most popular Python library for pulling data out of HTML and XML files. ## Installation ```bash pip install beautifulsoup4 lxml ``` *(We also install `lxml` because it is a very fast underlying parser that BS4 can use)* ## Creating the Soup ```python_not from bs4 import BeautifulSoup html_doc = """

Welcome!

Once upon a time...

""" soup = BeautifulSoup(html_doc, 'lxml') ```

slides.title: Finding Single Elements
slides.content:
# The `find` Method 🔍

The `.find()` method searches the tree and returns the **first** matching tag it finds.

```python_not
# Find the first <h1> tag
header = soup.find('h1')
print(header.text)  # Outputs: Welcome!

# Find by ID
title_elem = soup.find(id='title')

# Find by Class
story_elem = soup.find('p', class_='story')
# Note: We use class_ (with an underscore) because class is a reserved word in Python!
```

slides.title: Finding Multiple Elements
slides.content:
# The `find_all` Method 🕵️‍♂️ The `.find_all()` method scans the entire document and returns a *list* of all matching tags. ```python_not html = """
  • Apple
  • Banana
  • Cherry
""" soup = BeautifulSoup(html, 'lxml') # Find all
  • tags list_items = soup.find_all('li') for item in list_items: print(item.text) ```

slides.title: CSS Selectors
slides.content:
# Using CSS Selectors 🎨

If you know CSS, BS4 allows you to use CSS selectors via the `.select()` method!

This is often much faster to write than chained `find()` calls.

```python_not
# Find all elements with class 'item'
items = soup.select('.item')

# Find an element with ID 'title'
title = soup.select_one('#title')

# Find all <a> tags inside a <div class="nav">
links = soup.select('div.nav a')
```

slides.title: Knowledge Check: BeautifulSoup
slides.quizQuestion: Why must you use `class_` instead of `class` when searching by CSS class in the `find()` method?
quizOptions: Because 'class' is a reserved keyword in the Python language.
To distinguish it from the 'id' attribute.
Because BeautifulSoup uses underscores for all HTML attributes.

slides.title: Extracting Attributes
slides.content: # Getting Link URLs and Images 🖼️ Getting text with `.text` is easy. But how do you get the `href` of a link, or the `src` of an image? BS4 tags act like Python dictionaries for their attributes! ```python_not html = 'Click here!' soup = BeautifulSoup(html, 'lxml') link = soup.find('a') # Get the text print(link.text) # "Click here!" # Get the href attribute print(link['href']) # "https://google.com" # Get the class attribute (returns a list!) print(link['class']) # ['external'] ```

slides.title: Introduction to XPath
slides.content:
# What is XPath? 🗺️

While CSS selectors are great, they have limitations (e.g., they cannot select elements based on their text content, and they cannot navigate "up" the tree to a parent).

**XPath (XML Path Language)** is a query language designed specifically for navigating XML and HTML documents.

It is incredibly powerful and used heavily in advanced scraping frameworks like Scrapy and Selenium.

slides.title: lxml etree
slides.content:
# Using lxml for XPath 🌲 BeautifulSoup does *not* support XPath. To use XPath in Python, we use the `lxml` library directly. ```python_not from lxml import etree html_string = """

Hello

World

""" # Parse the HTML tree = etree.HTML(html_string) # Use XPath to find all

tags paragraphs = tree.xpath('//p') for p in paragraphs: print(p.text) ```

quizOptions: Select elements starting precisely from the root node.

slides.title: Advanced Predicates
XPath Axes
slides.content:
# Traversing Axes 🧭

XPath Axes allow you to navigate relative to the current node (up, down, sideways).

- `parent::` - Selects the parent of the current node.
- `following-sibling::` - Selects nodes after the current node at the same level.

## Example
Imagine a table without IDs, but you know the label "Price:". You can find the label, and then select the sibling element next to it!
```xpath_not
//td[text()="Price:"]/following-sibling::td[1]
```
This is an incredibly powerful technique for scraping difficult sites!

slides.title: Browser DevTools
slides.content:
# The Easy Way 🛠️

Writing complex CSS Selectors or XPaths from scratch is hard.

You can use your browser's Developer Tools (F12) to do it for you!
1. Right-click the element on the webpage and select **Inspect**.
2. In the DOM tree, right-click the highlighted HTML element.
3. Go to **Copy** > **Copy XPath** or **Copy selector**.

> ⚠️ **Warning:** Browsers often generate absolute XPaths (e.g., `/html/body/div[2]/table/tbody/tr/td[3]`). These are very brittle and will break if the website changes slightly. It is always better to write your own relative XPaths using IDs or Classes!

slides.title: Knowledge Check: XPath Capabilities
slides.quizQuestion: Which of the following can XPath do, that CSS Selectors CANNOT do?
quizOptions: Select elements based on their ID attribute.
Select the parent element of a known child element.
Select elements based on multiple class names.
Select the first child of an element.

slides.title: Summary
slides.content:
# Summary 🎉

You now know how to extract the needle from the HTML haystack!

## Key Takeaways
- ✅ **BeautifulSoup4:** The best tool for beginners. Parses HTML and makes it easily searchable using Python methods.
- ✅ **find & find_all:** BS4 methods to locate single or multiple elements.
- ✅ **CSS Selectors:** Use `soup.select()` for a concise way to query classes (`.class`) and IDs (`#id`).
- ✅ **XPath:** A powerful query language evaluated using the `lxml.etree` module.
- ✅ **Predicates:** Use `[]` in XPath to filter by attributes, index, or text content.
- ✅ **Text Matching:** XPath can find elements based on what they say using `text()="..."`.
- ✅ **Axes:** XPath can traverse backwards up the HTML tree to find parent elements!
